name: Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)
key_paper: Lim, B., Arik, S. O., Loeff, N., & Pfister, T. (2021). Temporal Fusion Transformers for Interpretable Multi-horizon Time Series Forecasting. International Journal of Forecasting, 37(4), 1748-1764. arXiv:1912.09363. Earlier version presented at NeurIPS 2019 workshop.
algorithm_description: TFT is a multi-horizon time series forecasting architecture that explicitly separates and processes three types of inputs: static (time-invariant) covariates, known future inputs, and observed past inputs. It uses Gated Residual Networks (GRN) with ELU activations and gating mechanisms to suppress irrelevant inputs, a Variable Selection Network (VSN) to identify informative features at each timestep, and a sequence-to-sequence LSTM encoder-decoder for local temporal processing. Temporal self-attention (interpreted as multi-head attention across the time axis) then captures long-range dependencies. Quantile regression heads produce prediction intervals rather than point estimates. The architecture was specifically designed for heterogeneous multi-entity forecasting where entities have different static properties (e.g., store type, region) that condition the temporal dynamics.
action_space_handling: TFT is a supervised forecasting architecture, not an RL algorithm — it does not natively define or sample from an action space. In a lottery-nn context, TFT would function as the policy network (actor) backbone that maps historical draw sequences and static lottery_id covariates to a probability distribution over balls. The output quantile heads can be repurposed as logits over the ball pool (N=50 for LottoMax), with sampling from the resulting distribution serving as the action selection mechanism. TFT does not natively handle combinatorial (set-valued) outputs — adapting it as an actor requires replacing the quantile regression head with N Bernoulli logits or an autoregressive masked sampler.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: TFT does not have a native mechanism for combinatorial k-of-N output. In a lottery-nn adaptation, the quantile regression head would be replaced by N logits (one per ball in the pool), and combinatorial constraint enforcement would be handled externally: (1) post-hoc Gumbel-top-k sampling from the N logits to select exactly k distinct balls; or (2) an autoregressive masking wrapper that calls TFT k times, masking already-selected balls at each step. The static covariate pathway (intended for entity embeddings like store ID) maps naturally to lottery_id embedding, conditioning the output distribution on which lottery is being played. Neither approach is built into TFT — both require custom wrappers around the TFT backbone.
sequential_generation_strategy: TFT's native output is point or quantile forecasts at multiple future horizons — it generates predictions jointly across horizons in a single forward pass (non-autoregressive in the horizon dimension). For lottery number prediction, this joint strategy translates to producing all N ball logits simultaneously in one forward pass (flat multi-hot generation). This means inter-number correlations in the output cannot be modeled natively — all N ball logits are independent given the encoder output. To model correlations (e.g., numbers that tend to co-occur), an autoregressive wrapper with k sequential forward passes and masking would be needed, but this is not how TFT was designed. The LSTM encoder-decoder inside TFT does capture temporal correlations across historical draws, which is TFT's actual strength.
gradient_estimator_type: TFT is trained with standard backpropagation through differentiable operations — it uses no discrete sampling during training. The quantile regression loss (pinball loss) is differentiable with respect to all network parameters. When adapted for combinatorial lottery output using Gumbel-softmax/Gumbel-top-k, a reparameterization estimator can be used to propagate gradients through the sampling step. For REINFORCE-based training (e.g., when TFT serves as an actor in an Actor-Critic setup), the score function estimator applies. The GRN gating mechanism uses sigmoid gates that are fully differentiable. TFT's native training does not involve discrete sampling, making it gradient-friendly when the output head is repurposed to produce continuous logits for downstream sampling.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: TFT has no built-in mechanism for combinatorial constraint enforcement (exactly k distinct numbers from {1..N}). Any constraint enforcement must be added externally: (1) Gumbel-top-k applied to the N output logits — draws k samples without replacement in a single differentiable operation; (2) autoregressive masking — iterate k times, setting the logit of already-selected balls to -inf before each sampling step; (3) post-hoc top-k selection — take the k balls with highest logit values (deterministic, non-differentiable, no diversity). The static covariate and VSN pathways naturally produce lottery-conditioned logits, but the constraint itself must be imposed by a wrapper, not by TFT itself.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium. TFT has more inductive bias than a vanilla transformer due to its LSTM encoder, GRN gating, and variable selection network — these components suppress irrelevant features and stabilize training on small datasets. The static covariate pathway reduces the effective variance each entity (lottery) introduces. However, TFT was benchmarked on datasets with hundreds to thousands of entities and time steps per entity; the paper's smallest benchmark (Favorita retail) has ~300K training samples. On 100-200 historical lottery draws, TFT is significantly over-parameterized: it typically has 500K-2M parameters vs. ~250K in the current SharedLotteryTransformer. Without aggressive regularization (high dropout, weight decay, early stopping), overfitting to 100-200 draws is likely. Rating: medium — better than a vanilla transformer of similar size, worse than simpler models like LSTM or GRN-only networks at this extreme small-data limit.
regularization_built_in: TFT includes several regularization mechanisms: (1) Gated Residual Networks (GRN) with ELU — the gating mechanism learns to zero out irrelevant features, reducing effective model capacity; (2) dropout applied within GRNs and attention layers (typically p=0.1-0.3); (3) variable selection networks learn sparse feature weights, effectively doing input regularization; (4) layer normalization in the GRN after gating; (5) skip connections (residual links) throughout, easing gradient flow and preventing co-adaptation. No explicit entropy bonus (this is not an RL method). The gating and sparsity via VSN provide the most meaningful regularization for small datasets, but dropout and weight decay still need to be tuned externally.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Documented and expected failure modes at n < 200: (1) Over-parameterization — a standard TFT has far more parameters than can be supported by 100-200 training samples; validation loss diverges or oscillates without heavy regularization. (2) Static covariate pathway collapse — with only 3 lotteries as static entities, the static embedding layer learns almost nothing useful; the entity-conditioned gating cannot generalize from 3 training entities. (3) Quantile head miscalibration — the pinball loss requires enough samples per quantile to estimate return distributions; with n < 200 there is insufficient coverage of the tail quantiles, producing degenerate prediction intervals. (4) LSTM encoder instability — the sequence-to-sequence LSTM component can diverge early in training when batch sizes are small, producing NaN losses; gradient clipping (max_norm=1.0) is required. (5) Attention collapse — with short sequences (20 draws of history), the temporal self-attention learns to attend uniformly, providing no benefit over the LSTM alone.
data_regime_evidence: TFT has not been validated on datasets with fewer than 200 training samples. Empirical evidence from original paper: (1) minimum_training_samples_tested: The smallest benchmark dataset in the original paper (Electricity, Favorita, Traffic, Volatility) has thousands of training steps per entity; the retail Favorita dataset has ~300K entity-timestep samples. No TFT paper validates below 500 samples per entity. (2) performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] — no published TFT degradation curve exists for n < 200; community experience (PyTorch Forecasting GitHub issues) shows TFT underperforming simpler models (e.g., N-HiTS, DeepAR) at n < 500 due to its high parameter count. (3) comparison_baseline: At small n, N-HiTS and DeepAR consistently outperform TFT in community benchmarks; TFT's advantage emerges at large entity counts and long horizons. Conclusion: TFT is empirically outside its validated regime at 100-200 lottery draws.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: No theoretical convergence guarantees exist for TFT at small n. TFT is a deep learning model trained with Adam optimization — asymptotic convergence to a local minimum is implied by standard SGD theory under learning rate decay, but no finite-sample bounds are published. The GRN gating provides implicit regularization that may prevent divergence but does not guarantee convergence to a useful solution. Empirically, TFT training on very small datasets tends to overfit within 20-50 epochs (validation loss stops improving before training loss plateaus), making early stopping essential. The LSTM component adds vanishing-gradient risk on very short sequences (SEQUENCE_LEN=20), though this is less severe than on much longer sequences.
reward_distribution_handling: TFT is a supervised forecasting model, not an RL model — it does not inherently handle reward distributions. In a supervised adaptation, the output can be interpreted as a probability distribution over ball numbers (using quantile heads or softmax logits), which implicitly models uncertainty. The quantile regression formulation is actually well-suited to the lottery's skewed draw distribution: different quantile outputs can model different frequency regimes (hot vs. cold numbers). However, TFT does not handle the 95% zero-reward sparsity of actual lottery play outcomes — that is an RL concept. If TFT is used as a supervised predictor (predict next draw numbers from history), reward sparsity is irrelevant; if used as an actor in an Actor-Critic framework, reward assignment and credit propagation must be handled by the surrounding RL training loop, not by TFT itself.
credit_assignment_granularity: As a pure forecasting model, TFT assigns no reward and has no credit assignment mechanism — it is trained on next-draw prediction targets using pinball or cross-entropy loss, where each individual number's presence/absence in the next draw serves as a label. This is equivalent to number-level (semi-bandit) credit assignment in RL terms: each ball logit is trained against a binary label (did this ball appear in the draw?). This is actually the most granular level of supervision and is an advantage of using TFT in a supervised fashion rather than with sparse play-level RL reward. If TFT is wrapped in an Actor-Critic loop, the surrounding RL algorithm determines credit granularity independently of TFT.
diversity_mechanism: TFT has no built-in diversity mechanism for combinatorial output generation. In its native forecasting use, TFT generates quantile predictions that span different percentiles, providing output diversity via the quantile regression head. In a lottery-nn adaptation, diversity must be introduced externally: (1) temperature scaling on the output logits before Gumbel-top-k sampling; (2) stochastic dropout at inference time (MC Dropout) to introduce prediction variance across multiple forward passes; (3) running k independent TFT forward passes with different dropout masks to generate k diverse plays. The variable selection network can learn to spread attention across multiple input features, providing some implicit diversity in which historical patterns are attended to, but this does not directly translate to diverse combinatorial outputs.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: TFT is natively a fully offline supervised learning model — it trains on a fixed historical dataset without any online environment interaction. This is the strongest compatibility advantage for the lottery-nn use case (one real draw per week). Training requires no live draws; the model learns to predict next-draw numbers from historical sequences. After each new real draw, the draw is appended to the CSV and the model is retrained (or fine-tuned) on the updated dataset — exactly the existing log -> train -> predict routine. No online RL loop is needed. If TFT is wrapped in an Actor-Critic framework, the offline compatibility depends on the surrounding RL algorithm (e.g., offline RL with CQL), but TFT as a backbone is fully compatible with offline training.
key_dependencies: PyTorch (already present); pytorch-forecasting (pip install pytorch-forecasting) — the primary open-source TFT implementation, depends on PyTorch Lightning; lightning (pip install lightning); optionally neuralforecast (pip install neuralforecast) for a lighter TFT implementation. A from-scratch TFT implementation without pytorch-forecasting requires ~800-1200 lines of custom PyTorch code for GRN, VSN, temporal attention, and quantile heads.
estimated_lines_of_code: 600-900 lines of new code for a from-scratch integration: GRN module (~80 lines), VSN module (~100 lines), static covariate encoder (~60 lines), LSTM encoder-decoder (~120 lines), temporal self-attention with interpretable weights (~150 lines), quantile/logit head replacement (~80 lines), data pipeline adapter for TFT input format (~150 lines), training loop integration (~160 lines). Using pytorch-forecasting reduces custom code to ~200-300 lines (data adapter + head replacement + training loop), but adds a heavy PyTorch Lightning dependency.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Low-to-medium compatibility with the existing SharedLotteryTransformer. TFT has a fundamentally different internal architecture (GRN + VSN + LSTM + temporal attention) compared to the Pre-LN transformer backbone currently in use — the two architectures cannot share weights directly. However, the lottery_id embedding concept maps naturally onto TFT's static covariate mechanism: the existing lottery_id embeddings (0=LottoMax, 1=6/49, 2=DailyGrand) can be fed into TFT's static encoder as entity embeddings without change. The draw feature representation (multi-hot + rolling frequency, 2*50=100 features per timestep) is compatible with TFT's expected input format. Practically, integrating TFT means replacing the SharedLotteryTransformer backbone rather than extending it, which means losing the pretrained encoder weights — a significant cost given the small dataset.
specific_application_in_project: TFT's most natural application in lottery-nn is as a replacement backbone for the SharedLotteryTransformer in a supervised next-draw prediction setting, not as an Actor-Critic component. Concretely: (1) TFT would replace model_swarm.py's SharedLotteryTransformer, taking draw sequences + lottery_id static covariate as input. (2) The quantile regression head would be replaced with N=50 binary logits (multi-hot draw prediction). (3) Training uses the existing BCE loss against historical draw targets — no RL required. (4) At predict time, Gumbel-top-k samples k=7/6/5 distinct balls from the logit distribution. The key TFT advantage is the static covariate pathway handling lottery_id more explicitly than a simple embedding add, and the VSN learning which historical features (hot numbers, recent frequency, gap patterns) are most informative. However, given the 100-200 draw constraint, TFT's over-parameterization makes it a worse fit than the current ~250K SharedLotteryTransformer. It is a Phase 3 candidate to evaluate if the dataset grows to 500+ draws.
replaces_or_extends: Replaces the SharedLotteryTransformer backbone in src/model_swarm.py entirely. Would require a new src/model_tft.py and updates to preprocessing_swarm.py to format inputs according to TFT's expected (static, known_future, observed_past) triple. Does not extend the current architecture — it is a full backbone swap.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. pytorch-forecasting (https://github.com/jdb78/pytorch-forecasting) — the most widely used TFT implementation in PyTorch, backed by PyTorch Lightning; includes the original TFT from Lim et al. 2021 with full quantile regression. 2. neuralforecast (https://github.com/Nixtla/neuralforecast) — Nixtla's forecasting library with a lighter TFT implementation alongside N-HiTS, PatchTST, and others; less Lightning overhead, easier to adapt. 3. GluonTS (https://github.com/awslabs/gluonts) — AWS's probabilistic time series library includes a TFT implementation in MXNet and PyTorch. 4. Original reference implementation by Google Research: https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/tft — TensorFlow-based, matches the paper exactly. 5. A PyTorch port of the Google reference: https://github.com/mattsherar/Temporal_Fusion_Transform — community-maintained, fewer dependencies. 6. Darts (https://github.com/unit8co/darts) — includes TFT as a built-in model with a clean scikit-learn-style API.
benchmark_results: From the original paper (Lim et al. 2021): (1) Electricity dataset (370 entities, hourly consumption): TFT achieves P50/P90 RMSE of 0.055/0.027, outperforming DeepAR, MQRNN, and N-BEATS. (2) Traffic dataset (862 time series): TFT P50 normalized deviation 0.094 vs. DeepAR 0.161. (3) Retail Favorita (largest benchmark): TFT achieves best quantile loss across all quantiles (0.1-0.9). (4) Volatility (financial daily returns, smaller dataset ~400 samples/entity): TFT competitive but not dominant vs. simpler baselines. Key finding: TFT's advantage over simpler models increases with the number of entities and the richness of covariates — it is least useful for single-entity short series, which is closest to the lottery use case. No published benchmark with n < 200 per entity.
notable_use_cases: 1. Retail demand forecasting (Favorita, M5 competition): multi-entity time series with static store/product covariates — structurally most similar to lottery multi-lottery prediction. 2. Electricity consumption forecasting: 370 consumer entities with temporal and static features — TFT's static covariate mechanism demonstrated on real entity heterogeneity. 3. Financial volatility prediction: short, noisy time series with heavy tails — closest data regime to lottery draws in terms of non-stationarity and small samples per entity, though TFT was not shown to dominate simpler models here. 4. Healthcare patient outcome prediction: patient-level static covariates (age, diagnosis) + temporal vitals — the static covariate pathway is analogous to lottery_id. 5. Traffic speed forecasting (METR-LA, PEMS-BAY): spatial-temporal multi-entity with known future covariates (time of day, day of week). None of these use cases involve combinatorial discrete output or sparse reward, so TFT's applicability to Actor-Critic lottery generation is indirect.
